newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil pushes through controversial sell-off.
newsitem.headline: Brazil pushes through controversial sell-off.

text.p: Brazil carried out Latin America's largest privatisation Monday, selling mining giant Companhia Vale do Rio Doce (CVRD) for about $3.2 billion despite opponents' rear-guard "guerrilla warfare" in the courts.

Planning Minister Antonio Kandir hailed the auction, won by Brazilian steelmaker CSN and its international partners, including Charlotte, N.C.-based NationsBank Corp., and said he was happy with the 19.98 percent paid above the base price.
"The premium was above expectations," Kandir told reporters. CVRD is a massive concern that owns ports, railways and mines iron ore, gold and bauxite, among others.

But even as the government celebrated the sale of the world's largest iron ore exporter, the slew of lawsuits that had delayed the sell-off from its original April 29 date continued unabated. A judge in Rio de Janeiro issued an injunction she said suspended the outcome of the auction.
Stock market officials said the injunction arrived too late to have any effect.

Jose Pio Borges, privatisation director of the National Development Bank which runs Brazil's privatisation programme, noted in remarks to reporters that the same judge had issued numerous injunctions before, all of which had been revoked.
But Brazil's attorney general was less sure, saying he believed the government would have to appeal the injunction before the auction was valid.
Earlier in the day, the barrage of court cases against the privatisation turned into high drama, with a court order suspending the bidding in midstride.

Waving a document in his hand, a court official strode onto the stock exchange floor in the full glare of a dozen television cameras and forced the government to call off the bidding as it reached 30.2 reais ($28.80) a share vs. the base price of 26.67 (about $25).
The sell-off only resumed some five hours later after government lawyers successfully requested that the injunction and another issued soon after be revoked.
Outside the Rio de Janeiro stock market where the auction was taking place, police in the morning set attack dogs on demonstrators who were throwing rocks and chanting abuse.

Local authorities said four policemen and two protesters were injured in the clashes, which were on a much smaller scale than the ferocious battles which took place on the original April 29 auction date.
Brazil hopes to raise some $5 billion with the privatisation of the jewel in its public sector crown, once the rest of the shares it owns are sold off.

But the sale has been fraught with controversy, with opponents ranging from former presidents to Roman Catholic bishops as well as leftists accusing Brasilia of selling off the country's mineral wealth for a pittance.
The government's plans generated an avalanche of more than 120 lawsuits, most of them filed at the last minute in what Planning Ministry officials have billed "guerrilla warfare".
